en: The Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra, Volume One;
appended to the Northern Liang Record.
At that time, the Buddha was traveling in Kapilavastu at the Śākya monastery, together with the great bhikṣus.
The assembly was gathered together.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself in salutation, and withdrew to stand to one side. With palms joined, she addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard that if a woman exerts diligent effort, she may attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa path. I pray that I may receive the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya."
"Because I have faith and joy while living at home, I wish to leave the household life to practice the Way.
The Buddha said,
"Wait a moment."
Kauṇḍinya! I do not delight in women entering my Dharma and Vinaya or donning my religious robes;

rather, they should, for the duration of their lives, purify themselves and fully cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), maintaining a tranquil mind and self-restraint without ever giving rise to conceptual thoughts. They should be serene like the Way, free from deviant thoughts or desires, and find their delight in the emptiness and stillness of the mind.
Then Mahāprajāpatī again entreated him, saying:
"May such a practitioner as this be permitted to do so?
We pray that the Buddha will grant us deliverance so that we may attain Nirvāṇa."
Thus he requested three times, but the Buddha would not grant his request; he then again prostrated before the Buddha, circumambulated him, and departed.
Not long after he had left, the Buddha, together with the great bhikṣus, proceeded from the Śākya hermitage and entered Kapilavastu.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī heard that the Buddha was coming from among his disciples into the kingdom; her heart was filled with great joy, and she immediately went to where the Buddha was. Joining her palms, she stepped forward to prostrate herself, bowing at the Buddha’s feet, and then withdrew to sit.
After a short while, she rose, knelt with palms joined, and stepped forward again to address the Buddha, saying:

"I have heard that if a woman exerts herself with diligence, she may attain the four stages of a śramaṇa. I pray that I may receive the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya, so that I may attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."
"Because I have faith and joy while living at home, yet I clearly understand impermanence, I thus desire to leave the household life to practice the Way.
The Buddha said, "Stop, stop."
Kauṇḍinya! There is no joy for a woman who enters my Dharma and Vinaya and dons my religious robes;

rather, she should, for the duration of her life, purify herself and thoroughly cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya). With a tranquil mind, guarding herself and never giving rise to conceptual thoughts, she should remain serene according to the Path, free from deviant thoughts or desires, and find delight in the emptiness and stillness of the mind.
Then Mahāprajāpatī again entreated him, saying:
"May such a practitioner be permitted to do so?
I pray that the Buddha will grant me deliverance so that I may attain Nirvāṇa."
Thus he repeated this three times, but the Buddha again refused to grant his request. He bowed once more, circumambulated the Buddha, and departed.
Overcome by a sense of grief and remorse, he was filled with sorrow and lamentation; tears flowed from him that he could not restrain.
She thought to herself:
"The karmic retribution for acting with the affectations of a woman is indeed like this.
She then immediately made a great vow:
"I pray that all bodhisattvas, as well as humans and non-humans, shall no longer harbor thoughts of this woman's nature.
From now on, we must seek Buddhahood, never becoming weary or indolent until the end of our lives."

At that time, the Buddha remained in this country with a great assembly of bhikṣus for three months to avoid the rain. Once he had finished mending his robes and completing his garments, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and departed from the country.
Mahāprajāpatī, together with the other elderly women, set out to follow the Buddha.

The Buddha traveled on until he reached the district of Nādikā and halted by a river. Mahāprajāpatī then went forward, prostrated herself in salutation, and having moved closer, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard that if a woman exerts diligent effort, she may attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa path; I pray that I may receive the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya."
"Because I have faith and joy while living at home, yet I clearly understand impermanence, I thus desire to leave the household life to practice the Way.
The Buddha said, "Stop, stop."
Kauṇḍinya! I do not delight in allowing women to enter my Dharma and Vinaya or to don my religious robes.

They should, for the duration of their lives, purify themselves with integrity and fully cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). With minds stilled and self-restrained, they should never give rise to conceptual thoughts; remaining serene as the Way, free from deviant notions or desires, they should find their delight in emptiness and stillness.
Then Mahāprajāpatī again entreated him, saying:
"May such a practitioner as this be permitted to do so?
We pray that the Buddha will grant us deliverance so that we may attain Nirvāṇa."

Thus he repeated this three times, but the Buddha again refused to grant his request. He then prostrated before the Buddha, circumambulated him, and departed. Retreating to stand outside the outer gate, he stood there wearing tattered rags, barefoot.
Tears fell like rain; his face and complexion were soiled and discolored, his clothes were stained with dust, and his body was exhausted; he sobbed and wept, unable to restrain himself.
He repented that there are eighty-four ways of indulging in evil conduct, which delude and confuse men, causing them to lose their virtue and the Way.
The Buddha knew this profound truth with such certainty: among the men of the world, there are none who are not led astray by women.
"Extremely difficult, indeed extremely difficult!
Because I now employ this manner of desire, I must purify myself and dare not let it fall into neglect.
Only you, my son, shall deliver your mother; in the end, you shall not fail your original vow."
Seeing that Mahāprajāpatī was thus unhappy, the venerable Ānanda asked her: "Kauṇḍinya!
For what reason are you wearing these tattered clothes and walking barefoot, with your face haggard and your body covered in dust, so exhausted and weeping in sorrow?"
Mahāprajāpatī replied, "Venerable Ānanda!
It is because I am a woman that I am unable to receive the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya; for this reason, I grieve for myself."
Ānanda said: "Stop, stop, Kauṇḍinya!"
Furthermore, please compose yourself and do not harbor further grief.
Wait until I have entered [the city] and shall speak of this matter to the Buddha, so that my mother may attain peace and be made joyful.
Mahāprajāpatī replied: "Ānanda!
Only you, O Worthy One, should see to it that she is granted transcendence and brought to full realization."

The worthy Ānanda immediately entered, joined his palms, knelt with his knees on the ground, and bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet. Having taken refuge three times, he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have heard from the Buddha that a woman who practices with diligence can attain the four paths of a śramaṇa.”
Now Mahāprajāpatī, with a sincere heart, desires to receive the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya.
Having lived as a householder, she possesses faith and joy;
she understands impermanence, has examined her own desires, and deeply realizes the truth.
"Now I wish to leave the household life to pursue the Way; I pray that the Buddha will grant me permission.
The Buddha said, "Stop, stop."
Ānanda! It is not possible for a woman who is driven by lust to enter my Dharma and Vinaya as a śramaṇa. Why is that?
This is because it necessarily endangers those of pure and lofty character. For example, Ānanda,
if a family of noble lineage has many daughters and few sons, one should know that the family’s prosperity is about to diminish.
"It will already be weakened and decayed, unable to achieve great flourishing.
Now, if women are allowed to enter my Dharma and Vinaya, it will certainly cause the pure conduct on the ground of the Buddha-dharma to be unable to abide for long."
Furthermore, it is like a field of rice where the grain is nearly ripe, yet a foul mist or calamitous vapor arises, causing the wholesome crop to be ruined and destroyed.
If women were to enter my Dharma and Vinaya, they would surely cause the pure conduct and Great Way upon the ground of the Buddha-Dharma to fail to flourish and prosper for long.
Why is this? Ānanda! It is further like a fertile and excellent field; if one takes seeds of thorny burdock and scatters them within it, that field will surely be ruined.
Now, to cause a woman to enter my Dharma is like this:

for a woman who enters the discipline of my Dharma, there is never a time when she can truly accomplish my Dharma; rather, she merely relies on my Dharma with the desire to ruin and destroy pure brahmacarya, thereby falling into the midst of sensual desire and establishing the very root of transgression.
Ānanda spoke again:
"Now, Mahāprajāpatī has many virtuous intentions toward the Buddha."
"From the time the Buddha was first born until he grew to maturity, his upbringing and nourishment were entirely due to the virtue of Mahāprajāpatī’s great love and joy.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
"There is such a person.
Mahāprajāpatī possesses great faith and many virtuous intentions; she has been of great kindness to me.
Seven days after I was born, my mother passed away, and it was Mahāprajāpatī who nurtured and raised me until I reached adulthood."

Now that I have attained the state of Buddhahood as the most honored one in the heavens above and the world below, and am known by the name Tathāgata, Unsurpassed, Truly Enlightened One, I also reflect upon those who have bestowed many benefits and virtues upon me; among them, I remember Mahāprajāpatī, whose kindness toward me is most profound and heavy.
It was solely through this grace that Mahāprajāpatī was able to come and take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus.

Furthermore, she came to have faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; she no longer doubted suffering, no longer doubted its origin, no longer doubted its cessation, and no longer doubted the Truths. Thus she perfected her path, perfected her faith, perfected her precepts, perfected her renown, perfected her generosity, and perfected her wisdom; she was also able to exercise self-restraint, refraining from killing, refraining from stealing from others, refraining from sexual misconduct with women, refraining from false speech to incriminate others, and refraining from drinking intoxicants that cause confusion.
Thus it is, Ānanda!

Even if one were to provide another with clothing, bedding, food and drink, seats and bedding, and medicines for the treatment of illness throughout their entire life, it would not equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of this merit and virtue.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If a woman wishes to become a śramaṇī, there are eight rules of respect that she must not transgress; she should study and uphold them for as long as she lives, maintaining them with personal discipline, faith, and understanding, and practicing them with single-minded devotion—just as one who guards against water carefully repairs the dykes and embankments so that no leakage occurs."
Those who are already able to act in this manner may enter the precepts of my Dharma and Vinaya.
What are the eight points of respect?

First, when a bhikṣuṇī who is a woman receives the true Dharma from a bhikṣu who upholds the great precepts, she must not treat him with frivolity, nor should she treat him with contempt, nor mock, deceive, laugh at him, or speak of trivial matters for her own amusement.
"Second, when a bhikṣu upholds the great precepts, a bhikṣuṇī who has been ordained for more than half a month must pay him homage and serve him.
She must not intentionally say, 'O new śramaṇa, are you weary from your diligent practice? Is it so cold or hot today? "
If there are those who speak such words, they will only confuse the minds of newly ordained bhikṣus.

One should always maintain self-reverence and diligent self-cultivation, encouraging and delighting the newly ordained to distance themselves from and guard against desire, remaining serene and self-composed.
"Third, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs must not dwell together or reside in the same place.
Should they dwell together or reside in the same place, it is considered impure; they will be entangled by desire and shall not escape the root of transgression."
One should firmly exercise self-restraint and clearly sever sensual desires, remaining serene and maintaining one’s own integrity.
Fourth, for three months one should stay in a single place to examine oneself; whatever is heard or seen, one should reflect upon and scrutinize it.
If one encounters false speech and does not respond, whether hearing it or not hearing it, seeing it or not seeing it, there will likewise be no conditions for coming and going.
One remains serene and maintains self-possession.
"Fifth, a bhikṣuṇī must not settle her own disputes through litigation.

Even if a bhikṣu, based on what he has heard or seen, should litigate with a bhikṣuṇī regarding what he has heard or seen, the bhikṣuṇī must immediately examine herself for faults and evils; she must not speak in a loud voice or use grandiose language to manifest her own lustful disposition."
"You should examine yourselves and maintain yourselves with serene composure.

Sixth, when a bhikṣuṇī aspires toward the Dharma, she may inquire of the bhikṣu-saṃgha regarding matters of the Sūtras and Vinaya; however, she may only discuss the Prajñāpāramitā and must not engage in discussing worldly matters that are not urgent."
If one speaks of matters that are not urgent, know that such a person is not practicing the Way; they are merely a worldly person given to negligence.
One should deeply examine oneself and maintain composure in solitude.

"Seventh, if a bhikṣuṇī has not yet attained the Way and violates the precepts of the Dharma and Vinaya, she must go before the assembly of monks every half-month to confess her transgression and repent, thereby casting off an attitude of arrogance."
Now, once again, she thus feels shame and remorse, deeply examining herself, remaining serene and self-restrained.

"Eighth, although a bhikṣuṇī may have been ordained for a hundred years and uphold the great precepts, she shall occupy a seat lower than that of a bhikṣu who has newly received the great precepts, and she shall pay him homage with humility and respect."
"These are the eight rules of respect.
I instruct women that they must discipline themselves and not transgress them; they should study and practice them for as long as they live."
"If Mahāprajāpatī can truly uphold these Eight Rules of Respect, she may be permitted to become a śramaṇī.
Having received the Buddha’s words, the Venerable Ānanda contemplated them with mature and profound discernment as being both deep and essential; he then rose, paid his respects, and departed.
She replied to Mahāprajāpatī, saying, "Kauṇḍinya!
You need no longer grieve or worry;
you have already received the permission to leave the household, and having departed home for the path, you shall find great peace and security."
The Buddha said:
"When women become śramaṇas, there are eight rules of respect which they must not transgress; they should simply study them with diligent intent throughout their lives and put them into practice."
"Maintain your mind as one would keep water out by properly repairing embankments and dikes, so that it does not leak away.
At that time, Ānanda explained to his mother, point by point, the Buddha’s instructions regarding the Eightfold Respectful Precepts, saying:
"One who can act in this manner may enter the Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha."
Upon hearing these words, Mahāprajāpatī was filled with great joy and said:
"Very well, Ānanda! Listen to my words."

For example, suppose there were a woman from one of the four castes who has bathed, anointed herself with fragrant unguents, and adorned herself with fine garments and ornaments; if someone further wished to benefit her, would she not thereby find even greater peace and security?
He replied, "There is nothing that is not peaceful. [The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, if one were to fashion a *pāyaka* (head-ornament) from fine flowers, incense, and precious jewels and give it to a woman, would she not cherish it and receive it upon her head?"

"Now, regarding these Eight Rules of Respect which the Buddha has taught and commanded, I too shall examine my own mind and vow to receive them upon the crown of my head and put them into practice; thus, I shall joyfully pursue this vocation without a single regret, binding myself in this way with nothing but gladness."
At that time, the Buddha conferred the ten precepts upon Mahāprajāpatī, ordaining her as a śrāmaṇerikā.
"For a śrāmaṇerikā who upholds the precepts, this is the severing of the roots [of unwholesomeness]:
one must not kill living beings; whether it be birds, beasts, insects, or moths, or when cutting trees, breaking branches, or plucking flowers, one must never harbor a harmful intent."
One must not steal or pilfer; one must not covet the wealth and property of others, nor indulge in sensual desires, nor employ soft and subtle speech to delude and confuse others.
To covet offerings for the sake of making them one’s own household business—such profit falls within the category of greed and theft.
“Bhikṣuṇīs should be careful and not involve themselves [in such matters].
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī received the ten precepts and became a śrāmaṇerī. “What are the ten precepts?
I shall explain the path for the worthy:

one should maintain a heart of loving-kindness and not give rise to poisonous intent. For as long as life lasts, one must not slaughter living beings or harm persons; one should always be mindful of those born and regard them with compassion.
Practice the Way with diligent effort, desiring to deliver your parents and all people; be careful never to seek vindication through litigation or to harm others.
Not even a single creature that flies, crawls, or moves about may be harmed.

Constantly desiring to save living beings with a compassionate heart toward the Way, one sheds tears upon seeing those who kill and abstains from eating upon hearing their cries, always remaining in a state of sorrow.
It is through such self-vows regarding the root of lustful desire that this state is attained.
Having made this resolve and attained this state, one must not give it to others.
To violate this precept is to no longer be a śrāmaṇerikā.
"Second, for as long as life lasts, one must not steal and must not covet wealth."
In buying low and selling high, whether by the *gui*, *he*, *zhu*, or *liang*, one must never deceive others.
Keep the mind fixed on the Way and maintain self-restraint with a tranquil will.
Do not instruct others to buy things, nor employ servants, borrow laborers, or hire clients. Furthermore, if others offer wealth, treasures, or male clothing and bedding, one must never accept them.
If one receives [such things], it will lead to impurity; this constitutes disorder.
One must not obtain clothing for adornment or robes made of precious jewels; one must not wear pearl rings or necklaces; and one must not sit upon high beds or within curtained canopies.
If one harbors such thoughts, it is impure.
Clothing is taken only to cover the body; do not seek out ornate patterns.

Food is taken only to fill the mouth and sustain the four great elements; do not be attached to flavors or accumulate filthy and base treasures. If people offer them, do not accept them—how could evil then find a way to advance?
If one were to accept such offerings, it would be impure.
Before preaching the sutras to others, one should extol the calamities of sinful karma and the sufferings of hell.
Worthy ones, you should know that the blessings of the heavens are immeasurable; do not speak contrary to this by discussing the affairs of worldly birth and death.
If someone offers a gift, it would be better to have one's hand cut off than to accept improper wealth; one should remain tranquil and self-restrained, firmly distancing oneself from sensual desire.
Should one violate this precept, one is no longer a śrāmaṇerikā.
"Third, a śrāmaṇerī must for as long as she lives refrain from sexual misconduct.

She must not keep a husband, nor think of a husband, nor dwell upon a husband. She must distance herself from men, restrain her passions, harbor no lustful thoughts in her mind, utter no flirtatious words with her mouth, and never allow flowers, incense, or cosmetics to come near her body."

Constantly contemplate that the state of desire is defiled, turbid, and impure; reflect upon your own evil inclinations and the myriad ways in which they manifest. It would be better to break your bones, shatter your heart, and burn your body to death than to die with lustful passion.
To live a life of lewdness is not as good as to die maintaining one's purity.
The state of lewdness is like Mount Sumeru: submerged within the ocean, there is no time of emergence.
The lust for sexual misconduct sinks one into the hells more deeply than Mount Sumeru.
Should one violate this precept, she is no longer a śrāmaṇerī.
"Fourth, a śrāmaṇerī shall maintain sincerity and faith throughout her entire life."

Sincerity is the foundation of the mind; let there be no duplicity in speech. One must not engage in double-tongued talk or speak of illicit and depraved acts. One must not utter foul abuse, slander others, or engage in idle chatter and flowery rhetoric—praising someone in one’s presence while disparaging them behind their back, or providing false testimony to implicate another in a crime.
One must not slander others, whether they be right or wrong.
Speak slowly and only proclaim what is correct; do not proclaim what is incorrect.
If one hears someone preaching the Dharma with a single-minded focus, one should contemplate its essential meaning and take it as a cause for celebration.
When a Great Being dwells in the world, an axe resides within his mouth; it is through evil speech that he brings about his own destruction.
To indulge one's mind and speak at will leads to calamity and misfortune; if one restrains body, speech, and mind, by what cause could disaster arise?
This is what the wise have realized: to maintain one's integrity with a single-minded focus.
Should one violate this precept, one is no longer a śrāmaṇerī.
"Fifth, a śrāmaṇerī must not drink alcohol for as long as she lives."
One must not taste wine, smell wine, sip wine, or give wine to others to drink.
One must not say that there are deceptive medicinal wines, nor go to a tavern, nor engage in conversation with wine-drinkers.

Indeed, wine is a poisonous medicine, wine is a poisonous water, and wine is a poisonous vapor; it is the source of manifold losses and the root of all evils. It harms the worthy and destroys the sages, brings ruin to the Way and its Virtue, and by causing slight contempt, it invites calamity and establishes the foundation of disaster.
The four great elements wither and decay; there is nothing that does not undergo change as one departs from fortune and turns toward calamity.
It would be better to drink molten copper than to drink the taste of wine. Why is this so?
Alcohol causes one to lose one's resolve, become deluded and insane, and leads one unconsciously into the hells; therefore, one must guard against alcohol.
Should one violate this precept, she is no longer a śrāmaṇerikā.

"Sixth, for as long as her life lasts, a śrāmaṇerī must not ride in carriages, on horses, or in litters; she must not indulge her whims or follow her own desires, nor may she utter insults or cast curses at will."

One must not play with five-year-old boys; one must not pull the trunk to touch a male animal; one must not strike or beat a male animal; and one must not grope or fondle the genitals of a male animal.
He maintained his will in tranquility, contemplating the Way of the sutras, and constantly took delight in emptiness and stillness.
Among all living beings, none die a happy death; yet he wished to purchase their flesh, for he did not eat the five kinds of meat.
One should always feel shame and remorse for the impurity of the foul secretions, repenting with a compassionate heart that causes no harm.
To violate this precept is to be no śrāmaṇerī at all.
"Seventh, a śrāmaṇerī must, for as long as she lives, not paint or draw."

One must not wear embroidery made with golden thread; one must not make woven garments to give to others; one must not sit on high beds or sit behind low curtains; one must not look into a mirror to examine whether one’s own appearance is handsome or not; one must not drape a bed with a coverlet; one must not sit haughtily upon a bed while chanting; and one must not speak while laughing loudly.
One must not speak in a loud voice; when speaking, one should use a gentle tone.

One must not play the lute or hold musical instruments; one must not sing or dance, nor shake one's body. One must not walk while looking back, nor walk while casting sidelong glances. One must not engage in buying or selling with commoners, nor dispute over profit or loss, causing others to slander [the teaching].
If one violates this precept, she is no longer a śrāmaṇerī. "Eighth:

For as long as her life lasts, a śrāmaṇerī must not study the arts of sorcery; she must not practice medicine or administer toxic potions to people; she must not speak of whether days are auspicious or inauspicious, nor engage in divining good or bad fortune by observing the calendar and celestial calculations, nor perform astrological computations regarding the waxing and waning of the moon, solar and lunar eclipses, the shifting and falling of constellations, landslides, earthquakes, wind, rain, floods, or droughts, nor predict the coldness or heat of the coming year."

One must not concern oneself with various illnesses, nor discuss the affairs of state, such as which country is strong and which is weak, or which people are robust and which are inferior; one must not speak of military expeditions, campaigns, conquests, or victories, nor of acquiring wealth and profit for the sake of one's household livelihood.

One must not speak of a certain family being wealthy and happy or another family being poor and suffering; one must not judge people by saying that such-and-such a mark indicates wealth or such-and-such a mark indicates poverty; and one must not cut down living trees to build one's own house.

One must not personally pluck fresh flowers with one's own hands to scatter over the Buddha. If someone brings flowers to offer to the Buddha, he should accept them and perform the ritual of *adhiṣṭhāna* (blessing) three times.

One should take pity on such people, for these flowers are but transformed flowers that cannot endure for long; all people are likewise like transformations, taking form from women and not enduring for long, yet sitting amidst suffering and pain.

Birth, old age, sickness, and death follow one another with mutual weeping and mourning; the mind is distressed and disordered, virtuous deities depart day by day, while malevolent spirits further harass them, until the body must die once more.
Therefore, it is like an illusion that does not endure for long.
Whoever violates this is not a śrāmaṇerī. "Ninth:
For as long as life lasts, a śrāmaṇerī must keep men and women separate and shall not reside in the same room; her path shall not follow after the path of a man."

She must not share a boat or a carriage with a man; she must not wear clothing of the same color as a man; she must not sit on the same mat as a man; she must not eat from the same vessel as a man; she must not dye fabrics together with a man; she must not cut or sew garments together with a man; she must not wash clothes together with a man; and she must not seek or beg anything from a man.

If a man presents fine goods as tribute, one should examine them with great care; one should distance oneself from what is suspicious and avoid what is doubtful, being prudent regarding the reputation of those one thinks of.
One must not engage in the exchange of letters or missives, nor act as a messenger on behalf of others.
If there is almsgiving, one should likewise not accept it.
If one wishes to travel, one must be advanced in years; take care not to travel alone.
When traveling, one must observe what is to be observed; should one see forms, regard them as impure.
"One must not go about separately or stay alone overnight in a single room.
Should one violate this precept, she is no longer a śrāmaṇerī.
Tenth: for as long as life lasts, a śrāmaṇerī shall not commit evil with her body."
The mouth commits no evil and the mind commits no evil; speech and action correspond with one another.
One does not befriend those who are not worthy and does not take as a master those who are not sages.
Why is it that one does not befriend those who are not worthy?
For the mind of the wise neither arises nor ceases.
Why is this? Because none but the sages are revered as masters.
Indeed, the sages possess no form of bondage or attachment, for they have extinguished and severed their lineage, and their defilements of greed are utterly exhausted.

Do not associate with or come and go from those who are disrespectful and unfilial, butchers, thieves, bandits, or those addicted to wine; their aspirations are perverse and dark, and their conduct is wicked and perilous. Be careful not to socialize with them, for those who do so will become defiled by their impurities and damage their progress on the Path.
One should maintain steadfast self-restraint.
One must not laugh loudly or engage in playful jesting; one must not run about in the presence of elders; one must not walk with the head held high; and one must not meet with kings too frequently.
If there is music and performance on the streets, one must not climb over walls to watch it, nor lean against a wall to watch it.
One must not sit with legs crossed, nor sit with legs extended, nor speak while reclining upon the seat.
"One should always feel shame regarding the impurities of women.
Should one violate this precept, one is no longer a śrāmaṇerī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kautamī received the ten precepts from the Buddha and did not fail in any of them.

He practiced the ten precepts without any leakage or deficiency. He remained constantly by the Buddha’s side for three years. Possessing intelligence and wisdom, he had extensively studied the various sutras;

he was joyful and undisturbed, his will as firm as a great mountain. His mind was upright and his intentions were correct, level and straight without deviance. He constantly felt compassion for all people and for every kind of creature, from those that fly and wriggle to those that crawl; there was none among them who did not sigh with sorrow [at their plight], and he exhorted and transformed them through wholesome dharmas so that they would ultimately be free from affliction and suffering.

For three years he had never committed even a minor transgression; returning once more to the Buddha, he prostrated himself to present his circumstances, bowing his head to repent for his faults and confessing everything without reserve.
The Buddha, with compassion and wisdom, instructed him on the afflictions of his offenses, establishing him so that he might be liberated from his evil transgressions.
I do not merely harbor resentment; I wish to offer these words:
the ten precepts alone are insufficient, for there remains more to be done.

After midday has passed, he must not go about walking through the streets and villages; once midday has passed, he must not eat again under any circumstances.
When walking in meditation within a room, one must do so according to the Dharma.
Should there be any who violate this, they are not worthy bhikṣuṇīs.
There are thirteen rules for a bhikṣuṇī entering a room.
What are the thirteen matters?
First, one should constantly reflect upon the impurity of the foul secretions; these delude people and entangle them solely in the roots of transgression, such that they cannot exert themselves.
Second, one should constantly reflect upon one's own transgressions and evils, realizing that one cannot return from them alone.
Third, one should constantly reflect upon the profound origins of one's offenses, realizing that one cannot emerge from them alone.
Fourth, one should constantly reflect upon one's own many lustful tendencies, realizing that one cannot purify them alone.
Fifth, one should constantly reflect that sensual desire disturbs the pure resolve for the Path, such that one cannot extricate oneself from it.
Sixth, one should constantly reflect that it destroys the intention for the Path, such that one cannot remain far removed from it.

Seventh, one should constantly reflect: "The mind is like a boat upon the water; if it seeks to carry too many people, it will suddenly sink into the water, causing all those on board to perish and unable to save itself."
Eighth, one should constantly reflect: "My mouth and tongue are crimson, which deludes the hearts of others; my mind is disordered and confused, and my eyes see nothing clearly.
Ninth, one should constantly reflect: "This body is like a silken bag used to hold foul excrement;
though its exterior is exceedingly beautiful, anyone who seeks profit from it or draws near to it will surely be defiled, as impurity flows forth with an unbearable stench."
Tenth, one should constantly reflect upon oneself: that one assumes an air of malice and strange pretenses, becoming arrogant and self-satisfied in an attempt to stir the hearts of others.
Eleventh, one should constantly reflect upon oneself: that one displays a weak demeanor, wishing to evoke pity from others, yet being unable to restrain oneself.
Twelfth, one should constantly reflect that having received a female form, one is bound by lustful dispositions and cannot liberate oneself.
Thirteenth, one should constantly reflect upon one's own reliance [on the body], which is impure and foul, and cannot free itself.
These are the thirteen matters for entering the chamber.
To conceal one's true state is an extremely grave offense.

If there is a courageous and defiant woman who observes her own mental states and desires and finds no escape from this affliction, she must contemplate deeply and realize the Truth (*satya*) in order to sever those states and desires.

Having extricated oneself, one practices the Way according to the precepts; relying upon the laws and regulations, one is composed and dignified in ritual conduct, and one’s speech accords with majestic decorum. Thus, one may swiftly attain a male body, as past consciousness remains intact.
Furthermore, by adding encouragement and support, and extinguishing all discursive thoughts, one may attain the stage of Srotāpanna;
one may also attain the stages of Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, or the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
If one does not realize [enlightenment], one shall become a Buddha after countless kalpas.
"There are four dharmas for a bhikṣuṇī entering a room. What are the four?
First, one should subdue one's own mind, refrain from thoughts of arising and ceasing, and keep the mind fixed upon the Way.
Second, one should exercise self-restraint, constantly discipline the mind, and direct one's will toward the Dharma.

Third, one should contemplate the impurities within oneself to eliminate mental afflictions; with a mind free from negligence, one should abandon sleep and reclining, diligently and strictly cultivating the self, refraining from arrogance and indulgence, and restraining oneself through self-guarding.

Fourth, one should establish the Dharma of the precepts so that all people joyfully follow them; [one must ensure they do not] become attached to the Buddha-dharma and abandon themselves to their own whims, becoming deluded by sensual desires, or [seeking to] seduce pure practitioners out of a desire for fame and reputation, thereby causing others to fall into calamity and misfortune.
"You must guard yourselves with care, so that the community may attain great peace.
Whoever violates this is not a virtuous bhikṣuṇī.
When a bhikṣuṇī enters a room, there are four rules of conduct."
What are the four? First, one should proceed directly with the head slightly bowed; one must not look left or right to compare oneself with others.
Second, one must not cough or spit upon the clean floor or the four walls within the chamber.

Third, one must not sit with legs crossed upon the bed where one stays; one must not lie on one's side on the bed; one must not prostrate oneself on the bed; and one must not lie flat on one's back on the bed.
Fourth, one must not stand with one's back to the bed where one rests, nor stand with one's back to the scriptures or images, nor stand with one's back to the fire.
These are the four matters concerning a bhikṣuṇī entering a room.
Reflect carefully upon this for yourself; you may thereby attain spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
If one violates this, they are not a worthy bhikṣuṇī.
"When a bhikṣuṇī enters a room, there are four rules of conduct."
What are the four? First, one should pay homage to the scriptures and images, as well as to the bed upon which one rests.
Second, one should sit upright and reflect within oneself; if one's demeanor is excessive, one should feel shame and remorse.
Third, when reading the scriptures and practicing the Way without weariness, one must sever all perverse thoughts.

Fourth, one should maintain a state of serene detachment, such that body, speech, mind, and intention are likewise; one should constantly keep in mind the desire to eliminate the affliction of these impure outflows.
These are the four.
One who commits these offenses is not a virtuous bhikṣuṇī.
"There are four further rules of conduct for a bhikṣuṇī entering a room."
What are the four?
First, one should always sit upright and must not lie down or gaze fixedly at the door.
Second, one should remain silent and rest in stillness, contemplating the Way of the sutras.
Third, one should close the eyes, close the ears, close the nose, close the mouth, close the body, and close the mind, settling the mind securely within emptiness.

Fourth, one must maintain firm self-restraint; one must not let the mind wander or act according to whim, nor allow the body to lean forward on the seat, pull up the robes to scratch oneself, or expose the physical form and various impurities and defilements so that spirits and deities may see them.
If ghosts and spirits were to see [such conduct], it would be a lack of reverence. These are the four.
Should one violate these, she is not a virtuous bhikṣuṇī.
"When a bhikṣuṇī enters a room, there are furthermore four rules of conduct. What are these four?
First, she should gaze straight ahead, maintaining a composed mind and free from improper thoughts."
Second, one should sit upright; one must not shake the body, nor shake the head or hands, nor shake the feet.
If one shakes them, the mind will be entirely unsettled and worldly dispositions will arise.
Third, one should maintain one's own resolve, guarding the eyes, guarding the ears, guarding the nose, guarding the mouth, guarding the body, guarding the intellect, and guarding the mind;
by guarding these eight, one can personally attain the Way.

Fourth, one must not call out to companions or engage in talk and laughter, nor discuss worldly matters that are not urgent, for even slight speech or loud laughter may disturb and disorder the pure resolve of the Way and its Virtue.
One should always maintain self-respect and not venture beyond the threshold by even three feet; how then could sin find its way in?
Should one violate this, they are no longer a virtuous bhikṣuṇī.

"When a bhikṣuṇī leaves her cell to relieve herself of urine or feces, she must inform the preceptor. The preceptor shall then dispatch two śrāmaṇerīs to assist her in adjusting her robes; the śrāmaṇerīs shall hold the inner folds of the *kaṣāya* for her as she exits, and once she has recognized the way back and emerged from the head of the chamber, she shall pay homage to the preceptor and depart."
One should not linger on the way; upon returning to the teacher’s quarters, one must do so without any further omissions or errors, and then depart after paying respects to the teacher.
Upon reaching the door of the room, one should snap the fingers three times. The śrāmaṇerikās shall all return to their teacher’s place and sit while performing walking meditation (caṅkrama).
This is the rule for a bhikṣuṇī when leaving her quarters.
Should she violate this, she is not a virtuous bhikṣuṇī.
When a bhikṣuṇī has gone out to the area behind the dwelling, there are ten matters [to be observed].
First, when one desires to defecate or urinate, one should go immediately; one must not allow these urges to remain pent up within the body.
Second, while walking, one must not look to the left or right, nor gaze at one's own private parts.
Third, upon entering the latrine, one should snap one's fingers three times.
Fourth, one should first ask the śrāmaṇerī:
"Is there no one here?"
The śrāmaṇerikā said, “There is none,” and then stepped forward.
If there is anyone present, one must not urge them to leave.
Fifth, having reached the latrine, one should snap the fingers three times;
when finished, one should again snap the fingers three times before descending.
Sixth, one must not swallow loudly.
Seventh, one must not lower the head to gaze intently at one's private parts.
Eighth, one must not play with the soil on the latrine.
Ninth, one must not pour wash-water against a wall.
Tenth, while the hands are still wet after washing, one must not handle any objects.
Should one violate these rules, it constitutes an unrighteous act.

"If a bhikṣuṇī has urinated, she must wash her hands and rinse her mouth, pay homage to the scriptures and images while deeply repenting, and also pay homage to her own bed; only then may she return to sit and practice walking meditation, contemplating and seeking the essential meanings according to the Dharma."
One should practice this oneself.
If one violates this, she is not a virtuous bhikṣuṇī.
"When a bhikṣuṇī leaves her room, there are three circumstances under which she may go out."
What are the three? First, one must go to the teacher to receive the scriptures.

Second, if anyone comes to see you, you must immediately go out to pay respects to the teacher as instructed by him, and then slowly meet with the visitor; you must not be more than two zhang away from the teacher’s location.
Third, when the midday meal is finished, one should rise and pay homage to the teacher;
these three matters require departure.
Should one violate this, she is not a virtuous bhikṣuṇī.
"When a bhikṣuṇī leaves the door of her chamber, there are three rules of conduct. What are the three?
First, when leaving the door, she should keep her head bowed and go straight out; she must not raise her head to look around in the four directions."
Second, one should move silently and must not indulge in loud coughing or spitting.

Third, one should exit the door slowly, reflecting with shame upon having received this female body—its foul impurities, its lustful dispositions, and its enmities—which bring about affliction, weariness, and suffering; such a womanhood is truly difficult to endure.
If one commits such an offense, she is not a virtuous bhikṣuṇī.
Thus have been explained the thirty-nine matters concerning entering and leaving the dwelling.
From the first month until the next, one should receive and uphold these rules of training without allowing any loss, maintaining them in silence.
"Next, I shall explain how to venerate it, so that people may quickly attain the Way.
The worthy Ānanda joined his palms, knelt with his knees on the ground, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"The laws and regulations for bhikṣuṇīs taught by the Buddha are likewise complete in themselves; there is no one who cannot attain deliverance through them."
"I fear that after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, there may again be women who become śramaṇas; would it then be permissible for them to act as preceptors for bhikṣuṇīs?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"If an elder bhikṣuṇī is fully endowed with the rules of training (śikṣāpada), it shall be so."
"Even so, it must be through the community of bhikṣus.
If the assembly can be obtained, yet even a single bhikṣu is unwilling, one cannot become a śramaṇa.
Ānanda again asked the Buddha:
“Is it because you have acted intentionally that you shall obtain the community of bhikṣus and become a female śramaṇa?
The Buddha said, “It is so.”
Ānanda! Why is this?
Women have many desires and affectations;

they only wish to delude others with their beauty and increase their number of disciples, yet they do not desire to study or inquire after the Dharma, knowing only matters of a momentary nature. For this reason, there must indeed be a community of bhikṣus.
Ānanda again asked the Buddha,
“Should one then cause a bhikṣu to act as a teacher?
The Buddha said:
"No. One should have a bhikṣuṇī serve as preceptor.
If there is no bhikṣuṇī, the bhikṣu-saṃgha may do so."
Ānanda again asked the Buddha:
"May the Buddha please explain at what age a female śramaṇā should receive the full precepts (mahā-śīla),
and at what age she should serve as a preceptor for novice nuns (śrāmaṇerikā)?"
At what age should one become a preceptor (upādhyāyī) for a śrāmaṇerikā?
At what age should one become a junior teacher (ācāryā)?
At what age should one become a senior teacher (mahā-ācāryā)?
At what age should one become an upādhyāya?
At what age should one accept invitations for meals from donors?
Regarding the place of residence, may it be within a stūpa or monastery?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What you have asked is profoundly deep and brings great transcendence.
Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it to you in full."
Ānanda said, "You should receive and contemplate this with careful attention.
At that time, Ānanda and the elder bhikṣuṇīs— Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the bhikṣuṇī Cilla, and others— all listened with single-minded devotion, their hands joined in reverence.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Since you have already accepted women becoming śramaṇīs, there will likewise be women who become śramaṇīs in future generations.
I shall now explain for you the dharma of the śrāmaṇerikās, to instruct those yet to come and those who have newly resolved their minds."
Desiring to become a śramaṇa and intending to cross over oneself by remaining far removed from the gates of transgression, one shall obtain a community of fifty bhikṣus and thirty bhikṣuṇīs;
if there are no bhikṣuṇīs, the number shall not be complete.
The assembly of bhikṣus invited by the teacher all took their seats; the women, having completed their prostrations, stood back with palms joined.
The teacher called for the women’s heads to be shaved, and once the shawls, robes, and sandals had been bestowed, he immediately conferred upon them the ten precepts, making them śrāmaṇerīs.
All should pay homage to the assembly of monks and say:
"I do not wish to entrust [the robe] directly to the assembly.
If his preceptor is seventy years of age or older, he should be ordained as a full monk.
A bhikṣuṇī who has received the threefold full ordination for five years should serve as a preceptor (ācāryā) for śrāmaṇerīs.
A bhikṣuṇī who has received the threefold full ordination for ten years should serve as a preceptor (upādhyāyā) for śrāmaṇerīs.
“A bhikṣuṇī who has received the threefold full ordination for ten years and possesses the full ordination should act as an upādhyāyikā.
A bhikṣuṇī who has received the threefold full ordination for fifteen years and possesses the full ordination should act as a mahopādhyāyikā.”
"A bhikṣuṇī who has received the threefold full ordination for twenty years may serve as an upādhyāyī for the full ordination.
The Buddha said:
"Even if a bhikṣuṇī is over seventy years of age, there are certain matters for which she must not receive the full ordination."
What are the various matters for which one should not receive full ordination?
One whose sensual desires have not been severed should not receive full ordination.
One who delights in anger should not receive full ordination.
One who delights in coming and going [restlessly] should not receive full ordination.
One who delights in fine wine and food should not receive full ordination.
One who delights in arrogance, loud voices, and shouting should not receive full ordination.
"One who can exercise self-restraint in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya will swiftly attain a male body and shall subsequently become a Buddha.
Ānanda asked again, "This is indeed truly difficult."
The Buddha said, "It is not difficult; it is simply that women create obstacles for themselves.
Ānanda asked the Buddha again:
"Is it appropriate for the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, who is of such noble character, to dwell among the mountains beneath trees or within stone caves?"
Should one dwell among hills, marshes, burial mounds, among people, or in private temples?
Should one accept invitations from donors to return for meals?
Should one provide medical treatment and rescue all people from illness?

I pray that the Buddha will explain each of these in their essential points, establishing the foundation of birth and death, so that those of future generations may all hear and know them, thereby establishing the Great Dharma; as when the Buddha was present, there were none who did not attain deliverance.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“There are also two causes and conditions.
Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain them fully for you, so that you may hold them well within your heart.”
If a bhikṣuṇī comes to rely upon my Dharma but is unable to return to it herself, then if she dwells among the mountains or beneath trees, the trees will wither and die.

If she dwells within a stone cave, the rock will crack and dry up, the trees will become parched, birds and beasts will suffer from hunger, the springs and wells will run dry, and the various māras will cause chaos.
If he dwells upon a mound or in a marsh, the grasses, trees, gardens, and fruits all wither and fail to grow.
If he dwells within a tomb, the dead will quarrel and compete with one another, causing heaven and earth to tremble.

If he dwells among humans, the land will be unstable; bandits and rebels will emerge in all directions, and military forces will not lay down their armor. The people will sigh in lamentation, all bearing the appearance of hunger.

If he dwells in a private monastery, he will cause the śramaṇas to become deluded by sensual forms, greedily attached to wealth and treasures, drinking wine and eating meat. They will clothe their bodies in fine silks and brocades, seeking physical beauty, while their ornate conduct and elegant gait cause them to lose the Way of the Sūtras. They will further slander one another and bring each other distress and affliction.

If one accepts an invitation for a meal from a donor, that donor will not obtain merit; instead, they will suffer many illnesses, their wealth will dissipate, their laborers will fall ill, malevolent spirits will arise more frequently, and calamities will increase day by day.
Why is this? Because these two offenses are directed against one another, how could the one who is ill ever recover?
For this reason, Kautamī and the bhikṣuṇī Citta and others, upon entering my Dharma, had five hundred years of their lifespan subtracted.
"Thus it is, Ānanda! Such are the faults and afflictions of women; you must receive and uphold this with careful attention.
Ānanda again knelt down with his hands joined in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How truly strange, how truly marvelous!
For what reason?
How could the offenses of a bhikṣuṇī be such as this?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"This is but a brief account from me.
Women possess eighty-four thousand hidden guiles that delude pure practitioners, causing them to fall into the hells, where they remain for many kalpas without being able to escape."
Yet there are eighty-four external manifestations that disturb the pure practitioner of the Way, causing confusion and delusion such that one loses the path of the scriptures.
Those who are deluded by women are all destined for the realms of the *niraya* (hells), *preta* (hungry ghosts), animals, and the hells.

At that time, when Ānanda heard these words spoken by the Buddha, he was greatly astonished and terrified; not knowing what those words meant, he lowered his head in dejection, and tears fell like rain, so that he could no longer move or stir.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not be afraid. I shall explain it fully for you, so that you may attain understanding and reach Nirvāṇa."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If a bhikṣuṇī dwells among the trees in the mountains and the tree withers and dies because of her, it is due to the many dissolute ways of women. With their coquettish glances, red lips, and crimson mouths, even when sitting beneath a tree they do not contemplate the Way; instead, they think only of the beauty of their own bodies and seek to seduce others, destroying people's wholesome minds and causing them to become deranged and lose their virtue and morality."
For this reason, the trees die and do not grow.

If a bhikṣuṇī dwells within a mountain cave and the entire mountain becomes parched by drought, the trees wither, the birds and beasts suffer from hunger, and the springs run dry, it is because women possess many lustful dispositions. Being foolish, deluded, and self-deluded, they do not contemplate the Way; instead, they think only of sexual desire, their minds finding no peace. Their sighing and weeping are more intense than their contemplation of the Way; though they outwardly explain the meanings within the sūtras, inwardly they harbor a heart of sensual passion.
Those who lament this are the views of the ignorant.
The wise know deeply that this woman does not contemplate the Great Way, but contemplates only other men; for this reason, drought has ensued and the springs have run dry so that nothing grows.
If a bhikṣuṇī dwells in a marsh, the birds and beasts within the marsh will devour one another, and the thorns and all the hundred grasses will wither and fail to grow. Why is this?

Because women abound in licentious airs and exclusively practice seductive delusions, they contemplate the origins and details of their reclining and rising; their minds thus give rise to thoughts from which they never again see the Way, losing their fundamental practice. From desire they bring about fetters, and once a poisonous intent arises, they see nothing before their eyes, and all demons manifest and cause them to tremble.
For this reason, thorns, weeds, and all vegetation were simultaneously caused to wither and die.
If a bhikṣuṇī dwelt among tombs, all the corpses within the graves would sit up and be subjected to flogging, and the cypress and pine trees of the burial mounds would all immediately wither and die.
Why is this? Because women are full of licentious airs; in stillness they do not contemplate the Way, but only contemplate sensual desire.
When a lustful mind and licentious demeanor arise, heaven and earth tremble, and all ghosts, spirits, and beasts are struck with fear.
For this reason, the cypress and pine trees at graves do not grow.

If a bhikṣuṇī dwells among the people, the kingdom will be in unrest; locusts will repeatedly appear, bandits and invaders will frequently arise, and the use of weapons and armor will never cease. The people will sigh in lamentation, and all will have the appearance of hunger.

Why is this? It is because women are full of capricious affectations; they are defiled by greed for physical beauty and lustful passion. They desire only to be respected by others and have no thought at all for the Way; instead, they think only of whether a man’s appearance is handsome or not, or whether a certain man is capable or incapable.
By day they engage in idle chatter and laughter; by evening they think only of sleeping and rising.
For this reason, the people are brought to poverty and distress, finding no peace or stability.

If bhikṣuṇīs reside in private monasteries, they cause the śramaṇas to become deluded by sensual forms, leading them to covet wealth and treasures, to drink alcohol and eat meat, and to clothe their bodies in silk and brocade to make themselves attractive. Their ornate conduct and elegant gait cause them to lose the Way of the Sūtras, as they proceed to slander one another and bring each other further grief and affliction.

Why is this? Because women are full of lascivious airs; they neither recite the sutras nor practice the Path, but merely produce soft and delicate sounds to delude men and cause their hearts to stir, so that those who have not yet attained the Way find their minds distracted.

They took turns examining one another and beheld their own impurities; seeing them all with extreme clarity—as if looking through a crystal—their minds were filled with joy and they calculated their immediate gain, but they immediately fell into birth and death, destined to become eunuchs for fifteen kalpas.
It is because of this that bhikṣus harbor mutual hatred toward one another.
If a bhikṣuṇī accepts an invitation for a meal from a donor, that donor shall not obtain merit; his wealth will diminish daily, and he will frequently suffer from illness.
Why is this? Because these women are full of wantonness and do not eat according to the Dharma; they merely act out their licentiousness in order to attract the gaze of others.
They do not consider the taste of the food at all, but only judge whether other men are suitable or unsuitable husbands.
In this way, although the donor intends to cultivate merit through giving, they instead incur a great transgression. Why is this?
Because they have come to eat with the intention of this bhikṣuṇī, not out of regard for the Dharma, but solely with a lustful mind.
For this reason, it causes the donor to find no peace or security.
If a bhikṣuṇī undergoes labor or illness, the patient will not recover, and malevolent spirits will further raise calamities that increase day by day.
Why is this? Because women are prone to many dissolute behaviors and cannot rectify their own minds; how then could they rectify the minds of others?
If they cannot even save themselves, how can they save others?
While one is under the sway of transgressions, how can one possibly liberate others from their transgressions? Why is this?
Because one employs excessive desire and harbors expectations.
"For this reason, they cannot cure the illnesses of others and cause spirits and deities to become disordered.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In my Dharma, there is currently a bhikṣuṇī who has just extended her lifespan by five hundred years."
After my parinirvāṇa, there shall again be three thousand bhikṣuṇīs and one thousand eight hundred bhikṣus who uphold this Dharma and Vinaya, and all shall attain arhatship.
In the final age, there shall be eighty thousand bhikṣuṇīs; among them, seven hundred and sixty bhikṣuṇīs will uphold this Dharma, Vinaya, and Sūtra, and all shall attain arhatship.
"As for the rest, after one hundred and thirty kalpas, they shall again uphold this Dharma and Vinaya, and they shall again attain arhatship.
At that time, Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"How should these bhikṣuṇīs practice in order to attain the Way?"
"What dharma should be practiced to achieve this?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Now, the defilement of lust in the world is exceedingly heavy; if one can sever this tendency, one may attain the Way."

The female body is like a precious jewel; its form is exceedingly beautiful, yet it cannot endure for long. It deludes one from the Way and its Virtue, causing the loss of the human state. Why is this?
Because of the excellence of the jewels, one would enter the deep ocean to seek them without ceasing, before long losing one's life.
When women seek the Way, they merely sit bound by the eighty-four external postures, which instead entangle their own bodies.
There are those who fall into eighty-four states, like entering a vast deep ocean where one's body is certain to sink.
Those who are able to eliminate these eighty-four states are Arhats.
Ānanda again joined his palms, knelt with his knees on the ground, and stepped forward to address the Buddha,
saying: "What are the eighty-four modes that prevent people from attaining the Way?"

I pray that the Buddha will exert his majestic spiritual power to explain this, manifesting his awe-inspiring virtue to inspire reverence; may all people understand and take joy in its meaning, so that by hearing it daily they may be liberated from the afflictions of transgression. May they attain the correct and true, thereby becoming joyful, and may those yet to come in the future likewise attain understanding.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; take it to heart, and I shall explain it to you in full.”
Thus it is, Ānanda!
Receive and uphold this with careful attention; explain its essentials to the bhikṣuṇīs of the future, the past, and the present, so that they may receive and uphold it.
"One who practices such a dharma will swiftly cause others to attain the Way.
The Buddha said:
"The eighty-four feminine guises are used to delude people and prevent them from attaining the Way."
What are the eighty-four manners?
A woman delights in rubbing her eyebrows and eyes to adorn herself; this is the first manner.
A woman delights in combing her hair and shaving her armpits; this is the second manner.
Women delight in applying cosmetics such as ointments and powders to delude men; this is the third manner.
Women delight in coquettish gestures and narrow-eyed glances; this is the fourth manner.
Women delight in red lips and crimson mouths; this is the fifth manner.
Women delight in wearing pearls and jewels in their ears; this is the sixth manner.
Women delight in wearing necklaces and gold beads beneath their necks; this is the seventh manner.
Women delight in wearing jewelry and garments of brocade and silk; this is the eighth trait.
Women delight in wearing woven sandals; this is the ninth trait.
Women delight in walking with their two arms swinging; this is the tenth trait.
That women delight in sidelong glances is the eleventh trait.
That women delight in sly glances is the twelfth trait.
That women desire to look at men but shrink back upon seeing them is the thirteenth trait.
When a woman sees a man depart and then looks back at him from behind, this is the fourteenth manner.
When a woman desires to see a man and, upon seeing him, lowers her head and remains silent, this is the fifteenth manner.
When a woman walks with delight, shaking her head and swaying her body, this is the sixteenth manner.
When a woman sits with delight, shaking her head and swaying her body, this is the seventeenth manner.
When a woman sits, lowering her head and rubbing her hands and nails, this is the eighteenth manner.
When a woman sits, she delights in speaking with a smile; this is the nineteenth manner.
A woman delights in speaking with a soft and gentle voice; this is the twentieth manner.
A woman delights in touching her two eyebrows; this is the twenty-first manner.
When a woman sits, she delights in barking loudly at dogs; this is the twenty-second trait.
When a woman sees a man approaching, she manifests great anger outwardly while feeling inward joy and delight; this is the twenty-third trait.
A woman who is arrogant and conceited, and who harbors hatred and jealousy toward others, is in her twenty-fourth state.
A woman who, desiring to win a husband, feigns anger upon seeing him, is in her twenty-fifth state.
When a woman sees her husband feigning anger, yet feels sorrowful and regretful in her heart even as he departs, this is the twenty-sixth trait.
When a woman sees a man coming to converse with her, she feigns wrath and reviles him while her inner heart is filled with joy; this is the twenty-seventh trait.
If a woman, upon seeing a man depart, slanders him with her mouth while her heart is filled with deep sorrow, this is the twenty-eighth trait.
If a woman is frivolous in speech, delights in reviling others, is impetuous, and persists in her errors, this is the twenty-ninth trait.
Women delight in being wanton and self-indulgent, considering others wrong while regarding themselves as right; this is the thirtieth trait.
Women are arrogant and treat the solitary and the weak with contempt, overcoming others by force; this is the thirty-first trait.
To use one's power and authority to intimidate others with the intent of gaining victory is the thirty-second trait of women.
To borrow without intending to return it, or to lend without intending to repay it, is the thirty-third trait.
That women delight in being crooked while claiming to be straight, and in being wicked while claiming to be virtuous, is the thirty-fourth trait.
That women are prone to anger and lack constancy, and that fools consider themselves sages, is the thirty-fifth trait.
A woman attributes virtue to herself while attributing faults to others; this is the thirty-sixth trait.
A woman claims credit for her own achievements while monopolizing them for herself and ascribing them to others; this is the thirty-seventh trait.
That women resent their own toil while rejoicing in the toil of others is the thirty-eighth trait.
That women take reality to be falsehood and delight in speaking of others' faults is the thirty-ninth trait.
Women delight in using their wealth to pride themselves upon others and their noble status to look down on others; this is the fortieth trait.
Women use their own poverty to envy the wealthy and their own low station to slander the noble; this is the forty-first trait.
Women delight in slandering others while flattering themselves and displaying their own virtue; this is the forty-second trait.
Women delight in ruining the achievements of others and destroying moral integrity; this is the forty-third trait.
That women delight in secret debauchery and bewitching delusions that lead them astray from the Right Path is the forty-fourth trait.
That women delight in harboring jealousy in secret, inciting agitation, and engaging in slanderous outbursts is the forty-fifth trait.
To criticize, disparage, and shift blame onto others—this is the forty-sixth state.
Furthermore, for a woman to speak falsely and slander those who are pure and upright in the Right Path, seeking to cause their ruin and confusion—this is the forty-seventh state.
Women delight in seizing upon the faults of others to delude their husbands; this is the forty-eighth trait.
Women delight in demanding that men take oaths to them and in bestowing favors upon others with the expectation of a reward.
These are the forty-nine states.
A woman delights in giving to others and then feeling regret, rebuking them, and disparaging those of high talent; this is the fiftieth state.
A woman delights in self-pitying complaints and reviling insects and animals; this is the fifty-first state.
Women delight in practicing seductive charms and sorcery to bewitch others; this is the fifty-second trait.
Women harbor resentment toward those who surpass them and desire that they die early; this is the fifty-third trait.
Women delight in holding poisonous drugs and administering them as lethal decoctions to others; their minds are not impartial—this is the fifty-fourth trait.
Women delight in constantly recollecting past evils, keeping them perpetually in their hearts—this is the fifty-fifth trait.
Women delight in following their own will and do not accept the admonitions of others; they are sycophantic, stubborn, and self-satisfied—this is the fifty-sixth trait.
Women delight in distancing themselves from those within and becoming intimate with those outside; they reveal secret matters to their neighbors and villages—this is the fifty-seventh trait.
Fifty-eighth: Women delight in being self-important, vexatious, and flighty; they do not rely on their husbands—this is the fifty-eighth trait. Fifty-ninth:
Women delight in being self-conceited, beating others without justification, and expressing anger or joy for their own sake, desiring to make others fear them—this is the fifty-ninth trait.
Women delight in the practice of lustful desire, acting with unrestrained authority, and seeking to oppose the True Dharma and contravene their husbands; this is the sixtieth trait.
Women delight in a lustful mind and harbor jealousy; they are full of suspicion and lack faith, harboring resentment and malice; this is the sixty-first trait.
Women delight in being irritable, squatting, and behaving disrespectfully while claiming it to be the Dharma; this is the sixty-second trait.
Women delight in using ugly words and evil speech without avoiding their own kin; this is the sixty-third trait.
Women delight in being arrogant, haughty, and self-indulgent; they treat the old and the young with contempt, showing no sense of hierarchy—this is the sixty-fourth trait.
Women delight in self-approval; they harbor malicious dispositions and ugly resentment, speaking without order—this is the sixty-fifth trait.
That women delight in laughter and do not avoid forbidden practices is the sixty-sixth trait.
That women delight in confining their husbands so that they may not speak or engage in playful banter with others is the sixty-seventh trait.
Women delight in being perverse and self-willed, and they treat men with contempt, speaking with lack of propriety and caution; this is the sixty-eighth trait.
Women delight in endangering others to ensure their own security, taking this as their pleasure; this is the sixty-ninth trait.
Women delight in slandering and harming the virtuous with malicious speech; their crafty and deceitful countenances delude and disturb the Way and its virtue—this is the seventieth trait.
Women delight in being artfully sly and flattering, claiming that others do not perceive it—this is the seventy-first trait.
Women who delight in greed suffer misfortune when they lose what they have gained;
they rejoice immediately upon gaining it, yet fall into sorrow and distress when losing it. They sigh and lament, blaming Heaven and speaking with disordered mouths—this is the seventy-second trait.
Women delight in reviling others, casting curses upon the hearth during wind and rain; they harbor malice, love killing, and lack a compassionate heart—this is the seventy-third trait.
Women delight in instructing others on how to cause abortions and do not wish for life to flourish—this is the seventy-fourth trait.
Women delight in peeping through holes and openings to observe others' physical traits, such as their height, and whether they possess wealth or not;
this is the seventy-fifth trait.
Women delight in flirtatious jesting, which inevitably deludes and misleads the minds of others; this is the seventy-sixth trait.
Women delight in teasing and harassing men, causing their minds to waver so that they cannot regain self-control; this is the seventy-eighth trait.
Women delight in extracting fetuses and dissecting bodies to observe their foul secretions; this is the seventy-ninth trait.
Women delight in laughing at those who are blind, deaf, mute, lame, or crippled; they take pleasure in themselves while disparaging others—this is the eighty-first trait.
Women delight in instructing others to divorce their wives so as to leave them in poverty and distress—this is the eighty-second trait.
Women delight in teaching others to strike and beat one another, conspiring to testify against each other; this is the eighty-second trait.

Women delight in teaching others to commit evil, engage in strife and litigation, and speak ill of one another to the authorities so that they may be imprisoned and confined; this is the eighty-third trait.

Women delight in inciting calamity and leading others astray; they laugh with deranged madness, and upon seeing them, people feel a sudden desire for them. Relying on their wild and violent nature, they forcibly seize the property of others, causing people to sigh in lamentation and say:
"Women are truly terrifying."
These constitute the eighty-four modes of behavior; one should clearly understand them.
If a woman can eliminate these eighty-four modes, there is none who will not attain deliverance, none who will not attain the Way, and none who will not attain Buddhahood.
The venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Can such lewd and lustful behaviors of women be eliminated?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This state is merely the work of women; if women were able to extinguish it themselves, they could certainly achieve its extinction.
'Extinction' refers to the Arhat of the present life."
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the heavens above and on the earth below, there is none who does not receive your compassionate salvation; all classes of living beings have attained liberation.
We pray that the Buddha will further explain and eliminate the afflictions of habitual desires, so that Mahāprajāpatī and the other bhikṣuṇīs may all attain understanding and release."
The Buddha said: "Excellent, Ānanda!
Listen attentively to what I say, reflect upon it well, take it to heart, and uphold it according to the Dharma, as a way of repaying the Buddha’s kindness."
"To act contrary to the Dharma is merely to exhaust women.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Ānanda and the elder bhikṣuṇīs all replied in unison, "So be it."
Receiving this with joy and reflection, she joined her palms and listened.
